words_to_read_new.meaning: com means together + mand means order: an order that pulls everyone together
de means down + mand means order: an order pushed down hard, not a request
mand means order + ate means to do: an official order to get something done
mand means order + ory means relating to: relating to an order, so no choice
com means together + mand means order + ment means the thing itself: the written order
com means together + mend means entrust: to entrust someone with your good words
com + mend means entrust + able means able to be: able to be praised
com + mend means entrust + ation means the act of: the act of praising in public
counter means against + mand means order: an order against an order, so it cancels it

associated_word_exceptions.reason: Ground 3 (OG_MEGA_PROMPT 4c): chosen instead of the card word remand because counter- was taught in Term 2, so countermand stacks a taught prefix on the new root and its sum (against + order) is fully transparent. remand needs the untaught re- and sits in adult legal register. remand is used on Tuesday's review grid instead.
associated_word_exceptions.source: Macquarie Dictionary (Australian English) countermand, verb: to revoke or cancel a command or order.

sessions.wtr_new_notes:
SAY: "Learn mand and mend once and every word about orders, rules and praise opens up for you as a reader and a speller."
READ each word as it appears, then connect mand or mend to the card meaning: order, entrust.
command - com means together + mand means order: an order that pulls everyone together. The captain commands.
demand - de means down + mand means order: an order pushed down hard. You are not asking any more.
mandate - mand means order + -ate means to do: an official order telling someone to get a job done.
mandatory - mand means order + -ory means relating to: relating to an order, so you have no choice at all.
commandment - com means together + mand means order + -ment means the thing itself: the written order itself.
commend - com means together + mend means entrust: to entrust someone with your good words, so you praise them.
commendable - com means together + mend means entrust + -able means able to be: able to be entrusted with praise. Worth praising.
commendation - com means together + mend means entrust + -ation means the act of: the act of praising someone in public.
countermand - counter means against + mand means order: an order set against an order, so the first one is cancelled.
Memory hook: MAND hides a hand - an order is put into someone's hand. MEND is that hand held out in trust, so it praises. Challenge: catch three mand or mend words in a school notice this week.
sessions.extension:
1. SAY: "When you finish, write one sentence that uses two mand or mend words and shows what they mean."
2. CHECK: the sentence must show the order or entrust meaning, not just use the word.
EXTENSION: Build the longest real mand or mend word you can, then write its full morpheme sum naming every part.
A morpheme sum names every part of the word and what each part means.
Answer: e.g. commandments = com (together) + mand (order) + ment (the thing) + s (more than one).

grammar.header_notes:
PURPOSE: Name the two halves of a complex sentence - the half that stands alone and the half that waits.
WHY THIS WEEK: in persuasive writing the opinion is one half and the reason is the other, and students keep leaving the reason on its own as a fragment.
ROUTINE: all grammar this week is written in the OG book. No boards and no scoring - books, thumbs and voices only.
PREP: main clause = stands alone. Subordinate clause = leaves you waiting. Same cover-and-read test every day.

i_do.title: One half stands alone
i_do.rule: A main clause stands alone. A subordinate clause leaves you waiting.
i_do.example:
Our canteen should sell fruit cups
because students get hungry by recess.
items: Cover one half. Read the other half out loud.
If it leaves you waiting, it is the subordinate clause.
i_do.footer: Tomorrow: which word makes it wait?
i_do.notes:
ANSWER: the main clause is Our canteen should sell fruit cups. The subordinate clause is because students get hungry by recess.
1. SAY: "Every strong persuasive sentence has two halves - your opinion and your reason - and today you learn to tell them apart."
2. WRITE: copy the whole sentence onto the class board as one line.
3. MODEL: cover the second half with your hand, read "Our canteen should sell fruit cups" and stop. Say it stands alone, then write MAIN under it.
4. MODEL: uncover, then cover the first half. Read "because students get hungry by recess" and stop dead. Say it leaves you waiting, then write SUB under it.
TRAP: choosing the longer half as the main clause. Fix: cover and read each half, hear which one waits, student re-labels it.
CLARIFY: if a student asks whether the main clause always comes first, say no - either half can come first, and we test by covering, never by position.
---
Purpose: day one names the two halves and gives the cover-and-read test. [I Do | Explicit modelling | Grammar | HITS 3]
PREP: a main clause is independent; a subordinate clause depends on it and cannot be a sentence by itself.

we_do.title: Which half is waiting?
we_do.rule: A main clause stands alone. A subordinate clause leaves you waiting.
we_do.example:
A) although the price would go up
B) our school should buy new library books
items: Thumb up for the half that stands alone.
Read it right to the end before you decide.
we_do.footer: Stem: A leaves me waiting because ...
we_do.notes:
ANSWER: B stands alone, so B is the main clause. A is the subordinate clause.
1. SAY: "Same test as the last slide. Read one half right to the end and listen for the wait."
2. TIME: 15 seconds thinking, voices off, then thumbs up for the half that stands alone, everyone, together, on three.
3. SCAN every thumb. 80%+ -> move on. Less -> read A aloud and stop dead so they hear the wait, then re-ask.
4. ASK: "What is A still waiting for?" 5 sec, cold call two students. EXPECT: what we should do although the price goes up.
TRAP: picking A because it sounds more grown up. Fix: read A aloud to the end, hear the wait, then re-signal.
CLARIFY: if a student says both halves make sense, agree that they do - then say making sense is not the test, standing alone is.
---
Purpose: guided use of the cover-and-read test on a persuasive pair. [We Do | Guided practice | Grammar | HITS 7]
PREP: A is a subordinate clause; although is what stops it standing on its own.

you_do.title: Main or sub
you_do.rule: Your turn: copy each half and write main or sub beside it.
you_do.example:
One done for you:
if we start a school garden = sub
items: A) every classroom should compost its scraps
B) because the bins are always full
you_do.footer: Check: does it leave you waiting?
you_do.notes:
ANSWER: A - main. B - sub.
1. SAY: "Look at the finished one first. Then copy A and B into your book and write main or sub beside each."
2. TIME: 90 seconds in your OG book. Work on your own.
3. CIRCULATE: to a stuck student say, "read it out loud and stop at the end - if your voice is still hanging in the air, it is a sub." Then do A together.
4. SCAN four books. 80%+ -> reveal the check slide. Less -> read B aloud together and hear the wait, then re-check.
TRAP: writing sub for A because it is long. Fix: read only A aloud, hear it finish, student changes it to main.
EXTENSION: Join A and B into one sentence, then rewrite it with the two halves swapped and the punctuation fixed.
HELP: Give students the two labels main and sub; they match each label to A or B and then say why.
---
Purpose: independent use of the cover-and-read test on persuasive halves. [You Do | Independent practice | Grammar | HITS 5]
ANSWERS:
A) every classroom should compost its scraps = main, it stands alone
B) because the bins are always full = sub, because leaves you waiting
EXTENSION: e.g. Every classroom should compost its scraps because the bins are always full. Because the bins are always full, every classroom should compost its scraps.
you_do.check_title: Tick it or fix it - main or sub
you_do.check_rule: Tick each correct label. Fix any label that does not match.
check_items: A) every classroom should compost its scraps = main
It stands alone, so nothing is left hanging.
B) because the bins are always full = sub

you_do.check_footer: Editing move: read each half on its own.
you_do.check_notes:

1. MODEL: "In A I read every classroom should compost its scraps and stop. Nothing is missing, so it is a main clause."
2. SAY: "Now tick each label that matches. Fix any label that is different."

4. SCAN corrections. 80%+ -> continue. Less -> read B aloud together, then re-check.
5. SAY: "When you write your persuasive paragraph today, check that every reason half is joined to an opinion half."
TRAP: ticking B because it sounds like a real sentence. Fix: read it alone, hear the wait, then correct it.

sessions.wtr_new_notes:
READ each word as it appears, then connect mand or mend back to the card meaning: order, entrust.
commander - com means together + mand means order + -er means the one who: the one who gives the orders.
commanding - com means together + mand means order + -ing means doing it now: giving the orders right now.
demanding - de means down + mand means order + -ing means doing it now: sending orders down without a break.
recommend - re means again + com means together + mend means entrust: to hand something on again with your praise attached.
commandeer - com means together + mand means order + -eer means one who acts: to take something by order, whether the owner likes it or not.
remand - re means back + mand means order: to order someone back, usually back into custody until the court sits again.
mandate - mand means order + -ate means to do: an official order telling someone to get a job done.
commandment - com means together + mand means order + -ment means the thing itself: the written order itself.
commendable - com means together + mend means entrust + -able means able to be: able to be entrusted with praise. Worth praising.
Memory hook: MAND hides a hand - an order is put into someone's hand. MEND is that hand held out in trust, so it praises. Challenge: catch three mand or mend words in a school notice this week.

grammar.header_notes:
PURPOSE: Name the one word that turns a whole clause into the waiting half.
WHY THIS WEEK: students write their reason as a fragment because they never notice the trigger word that makes it wait.
ROUTINE: OG books, thumbs and voices. No boards and no scoring anywhere this week.
PREP: because, although, when, if, since, while, unless, until are subordinating conjunctions. and, but, so are not.

i_do.title: The word that makes it wait
i_do.rule: The subordinating conjunction sits at the front of the subordinate clause and makes it wait.
i_do.example:
because students get hungry by recess
Cover because and the rest stands alone.
items: Trigger words: because, although, when, if, since, while.
Cover the trigger word. Does the rest stand alone?
i_do.notes:
ANSWER: because is the subordinating conjunction; cover it and students get hungry by recess stands alone.
1. SAY: "Yesterday you found the half that waits. Today you find the one word that makes it wait, and it is the word your reasons start with."
2. WRITE: copy "because students get hungry by recess" onto the class board.
3. MODEL: put your hand over because, read the rest aloud and stop. Say it stands alone now, then uncover and circle because on the board.
4. ASK: "So what is because doing to that clause?" 5 sec, choral response. EXPECT: it makes the clause wait for the other half.
TRAP: calling and or but a trigger word. Fix: cover and in Sam ran and Kim walked, hear that both halves still stand, student re-sorts it.
CLARIFY: if a student asks about but, say but joins two halves that each stand alone, so it never makes one of them wait.
---
Purpose: names the trigger word and adds the cover-the-conjunction test. [I Do | Explicit modelling | Grammar | HITS 3]
PREP: subordinating conjunctions make a clause dependent; coordinating ones (and, but, so, or) join two independent clauses.

we_do.title: Which one has a trigger?
we_do.rule: The subordinating conjunction sits at the front of the subordinate clause and makes it wait.
we_do.example:
A) although the queue is long
B) and the queue is long
items: Thumb up for the one with a trigger word.
Cover the first word. Does the rest stand alone?
we_do.notes:
ANSWER: A has the trigger word although, so A is the subordinate clause. B is not waiting.
1. SAY: "Both start with a joining word, but only one of them makes you wait. Read each one right to the end."
2. TIME: 15 seconds thinking, voices off, then thumbs up for A or fist for B, everyone, together, on three.
3. SCAN every thumb. 80%+ -> move on. Less -> read A aloud and stop dead, then read B and hear it finish, then re-ask.
4. ASK: "How do you know although is the trigger and and is not?" 5 sec, cold call two students. EXPECT: cover although and the rest stands alone, but covering and changes nothing.
TRAP: choosing B because and is a joining word too. Fix: cover the first word of each, hear which one is freed, student re-signals.
CLARIFY: if a student asks whether every clause has a trigger word, say no - a main clause has none, which is exactly why it stands alone.
---
Purpose: guided sorting of trigger words from joining words. [We Do | Guided practice | Grammar | HITS 7]
PREP: although is subordinating and and is coordinating; the cover test separates them without any labels.

you_do.title: Find the trigger word
you_do.rule: Your turn: copy each clause and circle the word that makes it wait.
you_do.example:
One done for you:
when the bell rings = when
items: A) unless we act now
B) since the tuckshop closed
you_do.footer: Check: cover it - does the rest stand alone?
you_do.notes:
ANSWER: A - unless. B - since.
1. SAY: "Look at the finished one first. Then copy A and B into your book and circle the word that makes each one wait."
2. TIME: 90 seconds in your OG book. Work on your own.
3. CIRCULATE: to a stuck student say, "cover the very first word and read what is left - if that suddenly stands alone, the word you covered is the trigger." Then do A together.
4. SCAN four books. 80%+ -> reveal the check slide. Less -> cover the first word of B together, then re-check.
TRAP: circling now in A because it is the last word. Fix: cover now, hear that A still waits, student circles unless instead.
EXTENSION: Finish both clauses into full sentences, then rewrite each one with the two halves swapped and the punctuation fixed.
HELP: Give students the trigger word list because, although, when, if, since, unless; they find which one starts each clause.
---
Purpose: independent use of the cover-the-conjunction test. [You Do | Independent practice | Grammar | HITS 5]
ANSWERS:
A) unless we act now = unless
B) since the tuckshop closed = since
EXTENSION: e.g. Unless we act now, the creek will keep filling with rubbish. The creek will keep filling with rubbish unless we act now.
you_do.check_title: Tick it or fix it - find the trigger
you_do.check_rule: Tick each correct trigger word. Fix any that does not match.
check_items: A) unless we act now = unless
Cover unless and we act now stands alone.
B) since the tuckshop closed = since
Cover since and the tuckshop closed stands alone.
you_do.check_footer: Editing move: check every reason has a trigger.
you_do.check_notes:
ANSWER: A - unless. B - since.
1. MODEL: "In A I cover unless and read we act now. That stands alone, so unless was the word doing the waiting."
2. SAY: "Now tick each trigger word that matches. Fix any that is different."
3. ASK: "Which of these two triggers would you reach for in a persuasive paragraph, and why?" 10 sec, turn and tell. EXPECT: unless, because it warns the reader what happens if we do nothing.
4. SCAN corrections. 80%+ -> continue. Less -> cover the first word of B together, then re-check.
5. SAY: "When you draft your persuasive piece today, start one reason with because and one with unless."
TRAP: ticking a whole clause instead of one word. Fix: point at the single circled word, student re-marks it.
---

sessions.wtr_new_notes:
SAY: "Learn jur, jud and just once and every word about fairness, courts and rights opens up for you as a reader and a speller."
READ each word as it appears, then connect jur, jud or just to the card meaning: right, law.
judge - jud means right or law: the person whose job is to decide what the law says is right.
jury - jur means law + -y means the group: the group sworn in to decide what the law says.
justice - just means right + -ice means the state of: the state of everything being right and fair.
injustice - in means not + just means right + -ice means the state of: the state of things not being right.
justify - just means right + -ify means to make: to make your side look right by giving reasons.
injury - in means not + jur means right + -y means the state of: the state of something not right being done to your body.
injurious - in means not + jur means right + -ious means full of: full of what is not right, so it does you damage.
prejudice - pre means before + jud means judge + -ice means the state of: the state of judging before you know anything.
judgemental - jud means judge + -ment means the act of + -al means relating to: relating to judging, so quick to judge other people.
judicious - jud means judge + -icious means full of: full of good judgement, so you choose wisely.
adjudicate - ad means to + jud means judge + -ate means to do: to act as the judge and settle it.
jurisdiction - juris means law + dict means say + -ion means the act of: the saying of the law, so the area where that court rules.
Memory hook: JUR, JUD and JUST are one family in three coats - law, judge, right. Meet a new one and ask: is this about what is FAIR? Challenge: find one in a persuasive text this week.
sessions.extension:
1. SAY: "When you finish, write one persuasive sentence that uses justice and shows what it means."
2. CHECK: the sentence must show the right or fair meaning, not just use the word.
EXTENSION: Write the full morpheme sums for injustice and prejudice, then write one persuasive sentence that uses both and shows the difference between them.
A morpheme sum names every part of the word and what each part means.
Answer: injustice = in (not) + just (right) + ice (state); prejudice = pre (before) + jud (judge) + ice (state).

grammar.header_notes:
PURPOSE: Put the two halves and the trigger word together and label all three in one sentence.
WHY THIS WEEK: a persuasive paragraph is opinion plus reason, and students need to see both halves in one sentence before they can build them.
ROUTINE: OG books, thumbs and voices. No boards and no scoring anywhere this week.
PREP: label M for main clause, S for subordinate clause, T for trigger word. Same three labels all week.

i_do.title: All three parts
i_do.rule: In a complex sentence: find the main clause, the subordinate clause and the trigger word.
i_do.example: We should ban plastic straws because turtles eat them.
items: Step 1: cover one half at a time. Step 2: name the trigger word.
Label them M, S and T in your book.
i_do.footer: Tomorrow: move the waiting half to the front.
i_do.notes:
ANSWER: M is We should ban plastic straws. S is because turtles eat them. T is because.
1. SAY: "This is the sentence shape your persuasive paragraph is built from - your opinion, then your reason - and today you can name every part of it."
2. WRITE: copy the whole sentence onto the class board, then draw a line straight down between straws and because.
3. MODEL: cover the right side, read the left aloud, say it stands alone, then write M above it. Uncover, cover the left, read the right, hear the wait, write S above it.
4. MODEL: circle because on the class board and write T under the circle, then say the board now shows M, S and T.
TRAP: labelling the whole sentence S because it contains because. Fix: cover the because half, hear the other half stand alone, student re-labels the left side M.
CLARIFY: if a student asks whether the trigger word belongs to the subordinate clause, say yes - it travels with it wherever the clause goes.
---
Purpose: brings the two halves and the trigger word together into one labelled model. [I Do | Explicit modelling | Grammar | HITS 3]
PREP: this is a complex sentence - one independent clause plus one dependent clause introduced by a subordinating conjunction.

we_do.title: Label it together
we_do.rule: In a complex sentence: find the main clause, the subordinate clause and the trigger word.
we_do.example: Homework should be optional if the work is already finished.
items: Thumb up when you have found the trigger word.
Then say which half is M and which half is S.
we_do.footer: Stem: The trigger word is ... because ...
we_do.notes:
ANSWER: M is Homework should be optional. S is if the work is already finished. T is if.
1. SAY: "Same three labels. Find the trigger word first, because it always sits at the front of the waiting half."
2. TIME: 15 seconds thinking, voices off, then thumbs up when you have the trigger word, everyone, together, on three.
3. ASK: "What is the trigger word?" 5 sec, choral response, then cold call one student for how do you know. EXPECT: if, because covering it lets the work is already finished stand alone.
4. SCAN every thumb. 80%+ -> label M and S chorally and move on. Less -> cover each half aloud together, then re-ask.
TRAP: reading if the work is already finished as a whole sentence. Fix: read it aloud and stop dead, hear the wait, student labels it S.
CLARIFY: if a student says the sentence works without the S half, agree - that is exactly what makes the other half the main clause.
---
Purpose: guided labelling of all three parts before students do it alone. [We Do | Guided practice | Grammar | HITS 7]
PREP: if introduces a condition, so the clause it starts always depends on the main clause to finish the idea.

you_do.title: Label all three
you_do.rule: Your turn: copy each sentence and label M, S and T.
you_do.example:
One done for you:
We need shade because the yard is hot. T = because
items: A) Students should choose their seats when the term starts.
B) Although the pool is cold, our swimming times improved.
you_do.footer: Check: did you circle the trigger word?
you_do.notes:
ANSWER: A - M is Students should choose their seats, S is when the term starts, T is when. B - M is our swimming times improved, S is Although the pool is cold, T is Although.
1. SAY: "Look at the finished one first. Then copy A and B into your book and mark M, S and T on each."
2. TIME: 2 minutes in your OG book. Work on your own.
3. CIRCULATE: to a stuck student say, "hunt the trigger word first - it is the one word you can cover to set a whole half free." Then label A together.
4. SCAN four books. 80%+ -> reveal the check slide. Less -> label B together on the board, then re-check.
TRAP: labelling B the wrong way round because the S half comes first. Fix: cover each half and read it, hear which one waits, student swaps the labels.
EXTENSION: Rewrite B with the two halves swapped, fix the punctuation, then write which order suits a persuasive paragraph better and why.
HELP: Give students the trigger words when and although already circled; they only label M and S.
---
Purpose: independent labelling with the subordinate clause in both positions. [You Do | Independent practice | Grammar | HITS 5]
ANSWERS:
A) M = Students should choose their seats, S = when the term starts, T = when
B) S = Although the pool is cold, M = our swimming times improved, T = Although
EXTENSION: e.g. Our swimming times improved although the pool is cold. Front position suits persuasion because the reader meets the objection first.
you_do.check_title: Tick it or fix it - label all three
you_do.check_rule: Tick each correct label. Fix any label that does not match.
check_items: A) M = Students should choose their seats, T = when
S = when the term starts, and it waits.
B) M = our swimming times improved, T = Although
S = Although the pool is cold, and it comes first.
you_do.check_footer: Editing move: name M, S and T in your own draft.
you_do.check_notes:
ANSWER: A - T is when. B - T is Although, and the S half comes first.
1. MODEL: "In A I cover when the term starts and read Students should choose their seats. That stands alone, so it is M and when is the trigger."
2. SAY: "Now tick each label that matches. Fix any label that is different."
3. ASK: "Why is B labelled differently from A even though both have two halves?" 10 sec, turn and tell. EXPECT: the waiting half comes first in B, so S is on the left and M is on the right.
4. SCAN corrections. 80%+ -> continue. Less -> relabel B together, then re-check.
5. SAY: "Pick one sentence in your persuasive draft today and mark M, S and T on it in the margin."
TRAP: assuming M is always the first half. Fix: cover and read, then re-label from what you hear.
---

sessions.wtr_new_notes:
READ each word as it appears, then connect jur, jud or just back to the card meaning: right, law.
adjure - ad means to + jur means law: to charge someone as if the law itself were asking. It is the strongest way to ask.
judiciary - jud means judge + -iary means the group or place: all the judges and courts of a country, taken together.
jurist - jur means law + -ist means a person who: a person who studies or writes about the law.
juror - jur means law + -or means the one who: one of the people sworn in to decide by law.
unjust - un means not + just means right: not right. Plain and hard, and useful in an argument.
justified - just means right + -ify means to make + -ed means it is done: shown to be right, with reasons behind it.
prejudge - pre means before + jud means judge: to judge something before you know anything about it.
judgement - jud means judge + -ment means the act or result: the decision a judge reaches.
misjudge - mis means wrong + jud means judge: to judge something the wrong way.
Memory hook: JUR, JUD and JUST are one family in three coats - law, judge, right. Meet a new one and ask: is this about what is FAIR? Challenge: find one in a persuasive text this week.

grammar.header_notes:
PURPOSE: Move the subordinate clause to the front and add the comma that shows where it ends.
WHY THIS WEEK: every persuasive paragraph that opens the same way sounds flat, and moving the reason to the front fixes it in one move.
ROUTINE: OG books, thumbs and voices. No boards and no scoring anywhere this week.
PREP: front position takes a comma, end position takes none. The trigger word always travels with its clause.

i_do.title: Move it to the front
i_do.rule: Move the subordinate clause to the front and put a comma after it.
i_do.example:
We should ban plastic straws because turtles eat them.
Because turtles eat them, we should ban plastic straws.
items: The trigger word always travels with its clause.
Front position needs a comma. End position does not.
i_do.footer: Check: comma after the waiting half?
i_do.notes:
ANSWER: both sentences say the same thing; only the second one needs a comma, and it goes after them.
1. SAY: "Shifting the reason to the front is the fastest way to stop every sentence in your argument sounding the same."
2. WRITE: copy the first sentence onto the class board, then draw a box around because turtles eat them.
3. MODEL: rewrite the sentence underneath with the boxed half first, so the class board now reads Because turtles eat them, we should ban plastic straws. Say the trigger word came with it.
4. ASK: "Where does the comma go, and why?" 5 sec, choral response. EXPECT: straight after them, because it shows the waiting half has finished.
TRAP: dropping the comma after the fronted half. Fix: read it aloud without the comma, hear the two halves run together, student adds it.
CLARIFY: if a student asks whether the comma is needed when the clause is at the end, say no - the trigger word already marks the join.
---
Purpose: models the move and the one punctuation rule it triggers. [I Do | Explicit modelling | Grammar | HITS 3]
PREP: a fronted subordinate clause is followed by a comma; the same clause at the end is not.

we_do.title: Comma or no comma?
we_do.rule: Move the subordinate clause to the front and put a comma after it.
we_do.example:
A) When the siren sounds we line up.
B) We line up when the siren sounds.
items: Thumb up for the one that is missing a comma.
Find the waiting half first, then check its end.
we_do.footer: Stem: A needs a comma after ...
we_do.notes:
ANSWER: A is missing a comma after sounds. B is correct with no comma at all.
1. SAY: "One of these is punctuated correctly and one is not. Find the waiting half first, then look at where it ends."
2. TIME: 15 seconds thinking, voices off, then thumbs up for the one missing a comma, everyone, together, on three.
3. SCAN every thumb. 80%+ -> move on. Less -> read A aloud with no pause so they hear the halves collide, then re-ask.
4. ASK: "Why does B need no comma at all?" 5 sec, cold call two students. EXPECT: the waiting half is at the end, so the trigger word already marks the join.
TRAP: adding a comma to B as well. Fix: read B aloud, hear it runs cleanly, student removes the comma.
CLARIFY: if a student asks about a comma before when in B, say no - that would split the sentence where nothing needs splitting.
---
Purpose: guided judgement on the one comma rule this week hangs on. [We Do | Guided practice | Grammar | HITS 7]
PREP: the comma marks the end of a fronted dependent clause; it is not used when that clause trails the main clause.

you_do.title: Swap and punctuate
you_do.rule: Your turn: rewrite each sentence with the waiting half at the front.
you_do.example:
One done for you:
We cheered because we won.
Because we won, we cheered.
items: A) Our library should open at lunch since the yard gets crowded.
B) Phones should stay in bags although some students disagree.
you_do.footer: Check: comma straight after the waiting half.
you_do.notes:
ANSWER: A - Since the yard gets crowded, our library should open at lunch. B - Although some students disagree, phones should stay in bags.
1. SAY: "Look at the finished one first. Then rewrite A and B with the waiting half at the front and the comma in place."
2. TIME: 2 minutes in your OG book. Work on your own.
3. CIRCULATE: to a stuck student say, "point at the trigger word, then copy from there to the end of that half first - the rest of the sentence follows after your comma." Then do A together.
4. SCAN four books. 80%+ -> reveal the check slide. Less -> rewrite B together on the board, then re-check.
TRAP: leaving the trigger word behind in the middle. Fix: read the new sentence aloud, hear the missing word, student moves it to the front.
EXTENSION: Write both versions of one sentence from your own persuasive draft, then write which version you would keep and why.
HELP: Give students the two fronted halves already written; they add the comma and copy the rest of each sentence after it.
---
Purpose: independent rewriting with the comma rule applied. [You Do | Independent practice | Grammar | HITS 5]
ANSWERS:
A) Since the yard gets crowded, our library should open at lunch.
B) Although some students disagree, phones should stay in bags.
EXTENSION: e.g. Because the bins overflow by lunch, we need a second one. We need a second bin because the bins overflow by lunch.

grammar.header_notes:
PURPOSE: Week review - name all three parts, then fix a complex sentence that is not working.
WHY THIS WEEK: fragments and flat openings are the two things that weaken a persuasive paragraph, and both are fixed by the same three labels.
ROUTINE: OG books, thumbs and voices. No boards and no scoring anywhere this week.
PREP: M stands alone, S waits, T is the trigger word. Fronted S takes a comma.

i_do.title: Everything in one sentence
i_do.rule: M stands alone. S waits. T is the trigger word. A fronted S takes a comma.
i_do.example: Although the canteen is busy, we should still sell fruit cups.
items: Cover one half at a time to find M and S.
The trigger word sits at the front of S.
i_do.footer: Where does that comma have to sit?
i_do.notes:
ANSWER: S is Although the canteen is busy, M is we should still sell fruit cups, T is Although, and the comma sits after busy.
1. SAY: "One sentence, everything from this week in it - and this is the exact shape that makes a persuasive argument sound like it has thought about the other side."
2. WRITE: copy the sentence onto the class board, then circle Although and write T under it.
3. MODEL: cover from Although to busy, read what is left aloud, say it stands alone, then write M above it and S above the covered half.
4. ASK: "Why is there a comma after busy?" 5 sec, choral response. EXPECT: the waiting half comes first, so the comma shows where it ends.
TRAP: labelling the first half M because it comes first. Fix: cover and read it, hear the wait, student swaps the labels.
CLARIFY: if a student asks which order is better, say both are correct - the fronted one is the one that answers an objection before you make your point.
---
Purpose: pulls the whole week into one labelled model. [I Do | Explicit modelling | Grammar | HITS 3]
PREP: a complex sentence is one independent clause plus one dependent clause; fronting the dependent clause adds a comma.

we_do.title: What is wrong here?
we_do.rule: M stands alone. S waits. T is the trigger word. A fronted S takes a comma.
we_do.example:
A) Because the oval floods every winter.
B) Because the oval floods every winter we need drains.
items: Thumb up for A, two thumbs for B, if it needs fixing.
One is missing a whole half. One is missing a comma.
we_do.footer: Stem: A is not finished because ...
we_do.notes:
ANSWER: A is a fragment with no main clause. B has both halves but is missing the comma after winter.
1. SAY: "Both of these turn up in real drafts all the time. Work out what each one is missing before you signal."
2. TIME: 20 seconds thinking, voices off, then thumbs on three, everyone, together.
3. ASK: "What is A missing?" 5 sec, choral response, then cold call one student for how do you know. EXPECT: a main clause, because covering nothing leaves it still waiting.
4. SCAN every thumb. 80%+ -> fix both chorally and move on. Less -> read A aloud and stop dead, then read B with no pause, then re-ask.
TRAP: calling A a complete sentence because it is long. Fix: read A aloud to the very end, hear the wait, student names it a fragment.
CLARIFY: if a student asks whether B is wrong or just untidy, say the missing comma makes the reader run the two halves together, so it counts as wrong.
---
Purpose: guided repair of the two errors this week is designed to prevent. [We Do | Guided practice | Grammar | HITS 7]
PREP: A is a dependent clause standing alone; B is a correct complex sentence missing the comma after its fronted clause.

you_do.title: Fix these two
you_do.rule: Your turn: rewrite each one so it is a correct complex sentence.
you_do.example:
One done for you:
Although it rained. -> Although it rained, we played on.
items: A) If we recycle our paper.
B) When the bell rings we pack up quickly.
you_do.footer: Check: one main half, one waiting half.
you_do.notes:
ANSWER: A needs a main clause added. B needs a comma after rings.
1. SAY: "Look at the finished one first. Then rewrite A and B in your book so each one is a correct complex sentence."
2. TIME: 2 minutes in your OG book. Work on your own.
3. CIRCULATE: to a stuck student say, "for A, ask yourself what happens - the answer to what happens is the main clause you are missing." Then write A together.
4. SCAN four books. 80%+ -> reveal the check slide. Less -> repair B together on the board, then re-check.
TRAP: fixing A by deleting If. Fix: say the trigger word is not the problem, the missing half is, student adds a main clause instead.
EXTENSION: Write one more complex sentence for your persuasive topic, then rewrite it with the halves swapped and both versions punctuated correctly.
HELP: Give students the ending we save hundreds of trees for A; they join it on and punctuate it.
---
Purpose: independent repair of a fragment and a missing comma. [You Do | Independent practice | Grammar | HITS 5]
ANSWERS:
A) e.g. If we recycle our paper, we save hundreds of trees.
B) When the bell rings, we pack up quickly.
EXTENSION: e.g. Because our bins overflow by lunch, the yard looks messy. The yard looks messy because our bins overflow by lunch.

you_do.check_footer: Editing move: hunt fragments in your own draft.
you_do.check_notes:

1. MODEL: "In A I read If we recycle our paper and stop. I am still waiting, so I add what happens, then put the comma after paper."

3. ASK: "Which of this week's three labels would have caught the mistake in A straight away?" 10 sec, turn and tell. EXPECT: M, because there was no main clause anywhere in it.
